title: PCA
story:
Measure enough things about the same objects and the measurements stop being independent. Height and arm span, six questions all probing the same attitude, forty sensors on one machine: the table has many columns and far fewer underlying quantities, and the extra columns are not extra information, they are the same information written down repeatedly.

Pearson's framing in 1901 is the clearest one and it is geometric rather than statistical. The paper is on lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space, and the proposal is to choose the line minimising the sum of squared perpendicular distances from the points to it. Hotelling gave the modern formulation in 1933, analysing a complex of statistical variables into principal components. The two descriptions — the direction of greatest spread, and the line of closest fit in the perpendicular sense — turn out to be the same direction, which is the fact the method rests on.

That word perpendicular is doing more work than it looks, and it is the distinction most worth taking from this lesson. Fitting a line by regression minimises vertical distances: the discrepancy is measured in the target's direction only, the roles of the variables are asymmetric, and swapping which one is the target gives a different line. This minimises distance measured at right angles to the line, treats every variable the same way, and gives the same answer however you label them. Regression predicts one variable from others. This describes the shape of a cloud. They are not the same operation and they do not return the same line.

Two consequences follow for anyone using it.

It is scale-dependent, in a way that is easy to miss because nothing complains. The directions are chosen by variance, and variance is measured in whatever units each column happens to use. A quantity recorded in grams will have a variance a million times that of the same quantity recorded in kilograms, so it will dominate the first component for no reason except its units. Standardising the columns first makes the answer about correlation rather than about measurement conventions, and that choice should be made deliberately rather than by default.

And the components are uninterpretable by construction. Each one is a weighted combination of every original variable, chosen for a geometric property with no regard for meaning, so it will usually correspond to nothing anyone can name. Reaching for a story about what component two represents is where this method most often gets misused — the axes were selected to capture variance, and variance is not importance.

problem.name: Principal components
problem.shape: Many measured columns describe far fewer underlying quantities, so the coordinates are redundant and correlated with one another.
tell: columns are strongly correlated with each other
there are more features than the problem plausibly has degrees of freedom
a visualisation is wanted of something with many dimensions
a downstream method is struggling with the number of inputs
problem.move: Centre the data, decide deliberately whether to standardise, and take the directions of greatest variance, which are also the directions minimising perpendicular distance. Keep as many as the problem needs rather than as many as a rule of thumb suggests, and resist naming them.
problem.invariant: The directions of greatest variance are the same as the directions of closest fit when distance is measured perpendicular to the subspace. That equivalence is what the method is, and it is why this is not regression.
problem.breaks: Variance is not importance. The method keeps the directions in which the data spreads most, which need not be the directions carrying the signal you care about — a low-variance direction can be the one that separates your classes, and it is the first thing discarded.

cost.time: a decomposition of the covariance matrix, cheap in the number of rows and cubic in the number of columns unless a truncated method is used
cost.space: the loadings, which must be kept and reapplied to any new data exactly as fitted
cost.beats: dropping correlated columns by hand, which discards information rather than combining it, and doing nothing, which leaves downstream methods to cope with redundancy

worked.problem: How is this different from fitting a line by regression?
worked.reasoning:
They minimise different distances, and everything else follows from that.

Regression minimises vertical distance. The discrepancy is measured only in the direction of the target variable, which makes the roles asymmetric: one column is being predicted and the others are doing the predicting. Swap which is the target and you get a different line, because you are now measuring error along a different axis.

This minimises perpendicular distance — at right angles to the line itself. No variable is singled out, all of them are treated the same way, and relabelling them changes nothing. Which is the formulation the 1901 paper gives directly: lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space.

So the two answer different questions. Regression asks how to predict this variable from those. This asks what shape the cloud has. Only one of them has a target at all, and asking for the better line is a category error until you say which question you meant.

The equivalence worth knowing is that the direction minimising perpendicular distance is also the direction of greatest variance. Those sound like different objectives and are the same one: total variation splits into variation along the line plus variation perpendicular to it, so minimising the second maximises the first. That is why the method can be described either way.

Two practical consequences I would add. It is scale-dependent, because variance depends on units — a column in grams has a variance a million times the same column in kilograms and will dominate the first component for that reason alone. Regression coefficients adapt to units; these directions do not, so standardising is a decision to make deliberately.

And the components are not interpretable by construction. Each is a weighted combination of every original variable, chosen for a geometric property with no regard for meaning. Regression coefficients attach to named variables and can be discussed; principal components usually correspond to nothing nameable, and inventing a story for component two is the commonest misuse of the method.

problem.practice: Take a dataset and compute the components twice, once on raw columns and once after standardising, then compare the first component's loadings. Afterwards, find a dataset with labels, project onto the top two components, and check whether the classes separate — then check whether they separate better on a component further down the list.

beats.broke: Many measured variables describe the same few underlying quantities, so the coordinates you were handed are more numerous than the structure they carry and are correlated with one another.
beats.fix: Find the directions along which the points vary most, which are the same directions minimising squared perpendicular distance to them — the geometric framing given in 1901 and formalised in 1933 — and keep the first few.
beats.cost: The directions are chosen by variance, which is a property of the units you happened to measure in, and the resulting axes are combinations of every original variable and so usually name nothing.

interview.q: How is this different from fitting a line by regression?
interview.trap: Treating them as two routines that both fit a line, one of which is better. They minimise different distances — perpendicular against vertical — so one describes the shape of a cloud symmetrically and the other predicts a designated target, and only the second has a target at all.
interview.answer:
They minimise different distances, and everything follows from that.

Regression minimises vertical distance: error is measured only along the target's axis, which makes the roles asymmetric — one column is predicted and the others predict it. Swap the target and the line changes, because error is now measured along a different axis.

This minimises perpendicular distance, at right angles to the line itself. No variable is singled out, all are treated alike, and relabelling changes nothing. That is the 1901 formulation directly: lines and planes of closest fit to systems of points in space.

So they answer different questions — how to predict this variable from those, against what shape the cloud has. Only one has a target, and asking which line is better is a category error until the question is settled.

The equivalence worth knowing is that the direction minimising perpendicular distance is also the direction of greatest variance. Total variation splits into variation along the line plus variation perpendicular to it, so minimising one maximises the other, which is why the method is described both ways.

Two practical consequences. It is scale-dependent, because variance carries units: a column in grams has a variance a million times the same column in kilograms and will dominate the first component for that reason alone, whereas regression coefficients adapt to units. And the components are uninterpretable by construction — each is a weighted combination of every variable chosen for a geometric property, so it usually names nothing, while regression coefficients attach to named variables and can be discussed.

takeaway: This minimises perpendicular distance and treats every variable alike, which is what makes it a description of a cloud's shape rather than a prediction of a target — and because its directions are chosen by variance, they answer to your units and to nothing you can name.
